newsitem.title: USA: Otis veteran gives China elevator business a lift.
newsitem.headline: Otis veteran gives China elevator business a lift.

text.p: After 50 years of working for Otis Elevator Co. in seven countries, Andrea Vecchiotti has literally had a career full of ups and downs.
But the most surprising twist is that Vecchiotti, who retired on Dec. 31, plans to spend his "leisure years" working for his former company in China.

Otis, the world's biggest elevator-maker and a division of United Technologies Corp., is in fierce competition in China with rivals Mitsubishi Electric Corp. of Japan and Schindler Holding AG of Switzerland.
Otis' market share in China is about 20 percent to 25 percent, placing it in a virtual tie with Mitsubishi and Schindler, an Otis spokeswoman said.
With its latest China venture, Otis is tapping an experienced manager to ensure the company's continued rise.

The Italian-born Vecchiotti, 65, said recently he will serve as advisor to an unspecified joint venture in China, where the elevator giant has already invested some $70 million in four joint ventures since 1984.
The company spokeswoman said that Otis would reveal details of the venture by the end of the first quarter.
Vecchiotti, who joined Otis in Milan, Italy, as a 15-year-old apprentice in 1946, has served in key manufacturing and engineering posts in Europe, Latin America and Asia.
He is not the first in his family to have answered the call of the elevator. His father worked for 20 years for the Stigler Elevator Co. in Milan, which was bought by Otis in the 1940s.
Vecchiotti's son, Alberto, is an engineer for Otis in Connecticut.
Vecchiotti was most recently Asia-Pacific vice-president of technology transfer for the Farmington, Conn.-based company.
He is studying Mandarin to round out the four languages he already speaks. Asked why he wants to learn Chinese, he shrugs, "You have to communicate."

He said one of his proudest accomplishments was helping build the company's $23 million factory in Penang, Malaysia, in less than 500 days. The factory, which opened in 1993, has already produced more than 2,000 elevators and 1,000 escalators, mainly for Southeast Asian customers.
He first went to China in 1987, where he helped transform what he called "primitive" production methods in Tianjin.
He said that while elevator technology had changed dramatically during his half-century in the business, not all of the changes were visible.

"What you see in the cab is not that different. Most of the change has been in the controls, in what you don't see," he said. "The big change is the microprocessor controls and the flexible software."

Vecchiotti, whose Singapore-based wife plans to join him in China soon, stopped in Connecticut just long enough for a celebratory glass of champagne with top company executives. They all agreed that China's potential market size is staggering.
"I think our Chinese company will one day be the biggest company at Otis," Otis Elevator President Jean-Pierre van Rooy said.
About 5 percent of the company's $5.3 billion in revenues now come from China, and the figure should grow to 10 percent by early in the next century, said van Rooy.
China accounts for more than 4,000 of the company's total 68,000 employees around the world.
The company sells about 41,000 elevators and escalators a year, and more than half of its new-equipment installations are now in Asia, said van Rooy.
